Confirm: encode the garbled string back to cp1252 and decode as UTF-8 — 'Renée' reappears; that round-trip proves the double-decode. Fix: decode the source as UTF-8 at ingestion (`open(..., encoding='utf-8')`, set the HTTP/DB charset), and repair already-stored rows with that same cp1252 to UTF-8 round-trip where it validates. Declare encodings explicitly at every boundary; 'platform default' is how this happens.
Partner's JSON upload is rejected: `Unexpected token is not valid JSON`. The file opens fine in their editor and the payload starts with an opening brace after an invisible character.

Cause: the file starts with a UTF-8 BOM — bytes EF BB BF, decoded as the invisible character U+FEFF before the `{`. Strict parsers (JS `JSON.parse`, many validators) reject anything before the opening brace. Confirm: hexdump the first bytes; `xxd file | head` shows `efbb bf7b`. Fix: strip the BOM at ingestion — read with `encoding='utf-8-sig'` in Python or remove a leading `\uFEFF` before parsing — and ask the producer to write plain UTF-8. Note the asymmetry: a BOM helps Excel guess CSV encoding but breaks strict JSON, so strip per-format, don't ban it globally.
Search for 'José' finds the account when typed on one device but not another, and we have two accounts that look identical: 'José' and 'José'. One was created on iOS, one on Android.

Cause: Unicode normalization mismatch. The same visible text can be NFC (single code point U+00E9) or NFD (e + combining acute U+0301) — byte-different, so exact-match search, uniqueness checks, and logins miss. iOS/macOS input often yields decomposed forms. Confirm: dump code points of both stored names (`[hex(ord(c)) for c in name]`) — one has `e9`, the other `65 301`. Fix: normalize to NFC on write and on query (`unicodedata.normalize('NFC', s)`, or a DB collation/normalized column), backfill-normalize existing rows, and enforce uniqueness on the normalized form. Case-fold as well if matching should be case-insensitive.
Posts containing emoji fail to save: MySQL throws `Incorrect string value: '\xF0\x9F\x98\x80' for column 'body'`, or silently truncates at the emoji. Table was created years ago with `CHARSET=utf8`.

Cause: MySQL's `utf8` is a misnomer — it's utf8mb3, max 3 bytes per character, so any 4-byte character (most emoji, some CJK ext. chars) can't be stored. The grinning face emoji is F0 9F 98 80, exactly the bytes in your error. Confirm: `SHOW CREATE TABLE` shows `utf8mb3`, and inserting an emoji into a test row reproduces it. Fix: migrate column, table, and connection to utf8mb4 (`ALTER TABLE ... CONVERT TO CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci`, plus `SET NAMES utf8mb4` / charset in the DSN), and check index length limits after the change — wider chars can exceed old key limits.
Signed callback URLs verify only sometimes. Failing ones contain names like 'Ann+Lee' or values with '%2520'; signature computed over the raw query string doesn't match what the receiver recomputes.

Cause: double encoding plus form-encoding confusion. A value encoded twice (`' '` to `%20` to `%2520`) decodes once to `%20`, not a space, so the receiver's canonical string differs from the signer's; separately, in query strings `+` means space (application/x-www-form-urlencoded), so a literal plus in a value becomes a space on decode. Confirm: decode the failing value twice and the signature verifies — that proves the extra layer. Fix: encode exactly once at construction, sign the exact bytes you send, use `%20` (not `+`) in signed components, and have both sides canonicalize by parsing then re-encoding with one agreed function before verifying.
Key lookups fail only for users on Turkish-locale machines: config key 'TITLE' lowercased in code doesn't match stored 'title'. The lowercased value contains a dotless i. Locale is tr_TR.

Cause: the Turkish dotted/dotless-I problem. In tr_TR, uppercase 'I' lowercases to dotless ı (U+0131), not 'i', so locale-sensitive case conversion corrupts ASCII identifiers — 'TITLE' becomes 'tıtle'. Confirm: run the same `.toLowerCase()` under `tr_TR` vs `en_US` — only Turkish produces the dotless form; setting the locale reproduces it on any machine. Fix: never use default-locale case ops on programmatic strings — use `toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)` / invariant casefold, or compare with a locale-independent canonical form. Reserve locale-sensitive casing for user-visible display text only.
CSV export opens garbled in Excel for accented names ('Renée' shows mojibake), but looks perfect in VS Code and Google Sheets. File is UTF-8, no BOM.

Cause: Excel on Windows guesses encoding when there's no BOM and assumes a legacy code page (Windows-1252), so UTF-8 bytes are misread — the same mojibake pattern as a bad decode. Sheets/VS Code default to UTF-8, hence the difference. Confirm: prepend the UTF-8 BOM (EF BB BF) to a copy and Excel renders 'Renée' correctly. Fix: for CSVs intended for Excel, write with `utf-8-sig` (BOM included) — while keeping BOM-less UTF-8 for JSON and machine consumers, whose strict parsers reject a BOM. Per-format encoding, declared explicitly, is the whole lesson here.
